OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF RAILROADS
STATE OF WISCONSIN
On the Commissioner’s Own Motion for a Determination of the 
Adequacy of Warning Devices of the BNSF Railway tracks with Ajax 
Road and Investigation into the Unauthorized Public Crossing of Winter 
Street in the City of Superior, Douglas County
9020-RX-186
FINAL DECISION
On September 16, 2024, the Commissioner of Railroads opened an investigation into the 
adequacy of warning devices at the grade crossing of the BNSF Railway (BNSF) tracks with 
Ajax Road (Crossing No. 082642N / MP 4.206) and Winter Street at NP Railroad fka Reiss Coal 
Dock Road (Crossing No. 082644C / MP 4.505) (Winter Street at NP Railroad) in the city of 
Superior. (PSC REF#: 517037.)
An Office of the Commissioner of Railroads (Office) investigator inspected the crossings 
in June 2025. At the Ajax Road crossing, the investigator recommended maintaining reflective 
crossbucks with Yield signs but separating the tracks into two crossings, each with its own 
warning devices. (PSC REF#: 583065.) At the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing, the 
investigator recommended replacing the Yield sign on the northern crossbuck assembly with a 
stop sign, maintaining the current reflective crossbuck and Yield sign on the southern approach, 
and installing supplemental crossbuck assemblies with Stop signs on the eastern and western 
roadway approaches. (PSC REF#: 572921.) No hearing was held.
The Commissioner ADOPTS the recommendation and ORDERS that the warning 
devices at the Ajax Road and Winter Street at NP Railroad crossings be upgraded and 
maintained as provided herein.

Findings of Fact
Ajax Road (Crossing No. 082642N)
1.
The Ajax Road crossing is a two-track crossing consisting of one industrial track 
to the north and one yard track to the south. The longest distance between the tracks, as 
measured along the roadway, is approximately 120 feet from outer rail to outer rail or 110 feet 
from inner rail to inner rail. The northern industrial track is rusty, overgrown with brush, and 
appears not to be used regularly. 
2.
Where the shortest distance between the tracks at adjacent grade crossings, 
measured along the highway between the inside rails, is more than 100 feet and less than 200 
feet, additional signs or other appropriate traffic control devices should be used to inform 
approaching road users of the long distance to cross the tracks1.
3.
The BNSF operates two through train movements per day over the crossing at a 
maximum timetable speed of 10 mph. 
4.
Ajax Road is 31 feet wide in the vicinity of the crossing with 27 foot pavement 
surface and 4 foot gravel shoulders and runs in a north-south orientation. The roadway intersects 
the northern industrial track at an angle of approximately 60 degrees with a left-hand-forward 
skew and the southern yard track at an angle of approximately 90 degrees. The roadway 
approaches to the crossing are level.
5.
Railroad Street runs parallel to the southern yard track in an east-west orientation 
and intersects Ajax Road between the two tracks. The intersection is 50 feet south of the 
industrial track and 32 feet north of the yard track.
1 MUTCD 8A.08.04 

Docket 9020-RX-186
3
6.
Winter Street runs parallel to the southern yard track in an east-west orientation 
and intersects Ajax Road approximately 120 feet south of the southern track.
7.
Ajax Road carried an average daily traffic (ADT) of 100 according to Wisconsin 
Department of Transportation (WisDOT) records at an unposted speed limit of 25 mph. During 
the inspection, the Office investigator noted that traffic was primarily industrial.
8.
A driver traveling at 25 mph on the northern approach needs a distance of 
196 feet to stop safely, and a driver traveling at 25 mph on the southern approach needs 175 feet 
to stop safely. The crossing warning devices are visible from more than 196 feet on the northern 
approach and more than 175 feet on the southern approach. The approach sight distance is 
adequate.
9.
Assuming a train speed of 10 mph, a driver traveling at 25 mph on the northern 
approach needs to see a train when it is 156 feet from the crossing from a point 196 feet down 
the highway, and a driver traveling at 25 mph on the southern approach needs to see a train when 
it is 147 feet from the crossing from a point 175 feet down the highway. The corner sight 
distance available in each quadrant from the safe stopping distance is as follows: 0 feet in the 
northwest quadrant, 65 feet in the northeast quadrant, 212 feet in the southwest quadrant, and 
90 feet in the southeast quadrant. The corner sight distance is inadequate in all four quadrants.
10.
At all crossings, except those with gates, a driver stopped 15 feet short of the near 
rail must be able to see far enough down the track, in both directions, to determine if sufficient 
time exists for moving his/her vehicle safely across the tracks to a point 15 feet past the far rail, 
prior to the arrival of a train. Required clearing sight distance along both directions of the track, 

Docket 9020-RX-186
4
from the stopped position of the vehicle, is dependent upon the maximum train speed and the 
acceleration characteristics of the “design” vehicle (WB-65 semi-truck).
11.
The necessary clearing sight distance at the Ajax Road crossing is 455 feet. The 
available clearing sight distance is 175 feet in the northwest quadrant but over 2000 feet in the 
remaining quadrants. The clearing sight distance is inadequate in the northwest quadrant.
12.
Wisconsin Stat. § 195.29(6) requires railroads, municipalities, and persons 
owning or occupying land adjacent to any railroad-highway grade crossing to keep sight 
triangles formed by the intersecting points 330 feet down the tracks and highway in each 
direction clear of trees and brush to provide an adequate view of approaching trains from the 
highway.
13.
At the time of the inspection, brush clearing was needed in the northeast and 
northwest quadrants on property owned by BNSF.
14.
The exposure factor at this crossing is 200. The exposure factor is the number of 
trains multiplied by vehicles per day, showing the potential conflicts at the crossing.
15.
No train-vehicle accidents have occurred at this crossing since 1973.
16.
An Advance Warning Sign (W10-1) (AWS) is required to be installed at all 
at-grade highway crossings, unless specifically not required by the Manual on Uniform Traffic 
Control Devices (MUTCD) § 8B.06.
17.
AWS were not present at the time of the inspection.

Docket 9020-RX-186
5
18.
A “parallel tracks” advance warning sign (W10-2, W10-3, or W10-4) is required 
to be installed on each approach of a parallel highway adjacent to an at-grade highway crossing 
where the distance between the tracks and the parallel highway is less than 100 feet.2
19.
Parallel tracks advance warning signs were not present on eastbound Railroad 
Street at the time of the inspection.
20.
Pavement markings are not required at this crossing. The use of yield and stop 
lines should adhere to the standards and guidance in the WMUTCD3. 
21.
The WisDOT has produced a benefit-cost analysis for all at-grade crossings in the 
state. Installing new automatic flashing lights with gates and constant warning time circuitry at 
the Ajax Road crossing would have a net benefit of about -$396,200. The benefit-cost ratio is 
about 0.02, meaning that the public would receive about $0.02 in safety benefits for each dollar 
expended.
22.
At the time of the inspection, there were not any traffic control or railroad 
warning devices visible to drivers turning from eastbound Railroad Street to northbound or 
southbound Ajax Road.
23.
The crossing is presently protected with reflective crossbucks and Yield signs. 
Conditions warrant maintaining the warning devices at this crossing because of the low train and 
vehicle speeds, low exposure factor, and low net benefit. To promote public safety, it is 
necessary to separate the industrial track and yard track into individual crossings, and install and 
maintain a set of reflective crossbucks with Yield signs at each crossing.

3 WMUTCD 2023 8C.03.01, 8C.03.02 and 8C.03.03 (crossings with passive warning devices).

6
Winter Street at NP Railroad (Crossing No. 082644C)
24.
The Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing is a three-track crossing consisting of 
one industrial track to the north and two yard tracks to the south. The longest distance between 
the northernmost and southernmost tracks, as measured along NP Railroad, is approximately 
55 feet from outer rail to outer rail.
25.
The Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing is classified as a private crossing in the 
U.S. DOT inventory; however, the Douglas County GIS Map indicates that the road through the 
NP Railroad crossing is a public road. A new public crossing requires Office approval under 
Wis. Stat. §§ 195.28 and 195.29. The City did not seek approval for the establishment of the NP 
Railroad public crossing.
26.
The BNSF operates one train movement per week over the crossing at a 
maximum timetable speed of 10 mph. 
27.
NP Railroad is 30 feet wide in the vicinity of the crossing and runs in a north-
south orientation. NP Railroad forms a T-intersection at its southern terminus with Winter 
Street, which runs in an east-west orientation, and a four-way intersection with Railroad Street to 
the north, which runs in an east-west orientation. The distance between these intersections is 
approximately 132 feet. NP Railroad is unpaved except at the crossing and the Railroad Street 
intersection.
28.
The two southern yard tracks run between Railroad Street and Winter Street and 
intersect NP Railroad at an angle of approximately 90 degrees. The southernmost track is 
approximately 90 feet north of the Winter Street intersection. East of the crossing, the northern 

Docket 9020-RX-186
7
industrial track diverges from the yard track through the intersection of NP Railroad and 
Railroad Street. 
29.
NP Railroad intersects the northern industrial track at an angle of approximately 
76 degrees with a left-hand-forward skew. The northern roadway approach is level, and the 
southern roadway approach declines by one percent.
30.
Railroad Street intersects the northern industrial track at an angle of 
approximately 16 degrees with a right-hand-forward skew. Both the eastern and western 
roadway approaches are level.
31.
NP Railroad has an unposted speed limit of 25 mph. During the inspection, the 
Office investigator noted that traffic was primarily industrial.
32.
A driver traveling at 25 mph on NP Railroad needs 175 feet to stop safely. The 
crossing warning devices are visible from more than 175 feet on the northern approach and from 
the intersection of Winter Street at NP Railroad. The approach sight distance is adequate on NP 
Railroad.
33.
A driver traveling at 25 mph on Railroad Street needs 288 feet to stop safely. The 
crossing warning devices are visible from more than 288 feet on each Railroad Street approach. 
The approach sight distance is adequate on Railroad Street.
34.
Assuming a train speed of 10 mph, a driver traveling at 25 mph on NP Railroad 
needs to see a train when it is 121 feet from the crossing from a point 175 feet down the 
highway. The corner sight distance available in each quadrant from the safe stopping distance on 
NP Railroad is as follows: 30 feet in the northwest quadrant, 110 feet in the northeast quadrant, 

Docket 9020-RX-186
8
100 feet in the southwest quadrant, and 45 feet in the southeast quadrant. The corner sight 
distance is inadequate in all four quadrants from NP Railroad.
35.
Assuming a train speed of 10 mph, a driver traveling at 25 mph on Railroad Street 
needs to see a train when it is 162 feet from the crossing from a point 288 feet down the 
highway. The corner sight distance available in each quadrant from the safe stopping distance on 
Railroad Street is as follows: 134 feet in the northwest quadrant, 150 feet in the northeast 
quadrant, 2,000+ feet in the southwest quadrant, and 2,000+ feet in the southeast quadrant. The 
corner sight distance is inadequate in the northwest and northeast quadrants from Railroad Street.
36.
At all crossings, except those with gates, a driver stopped 15 feet short of the near 
rail must be able to see far enough down the track, in both directions, to determine if sufficient 
time exists for moving his/her vehicle safely across the tracks to a point 15 feet past the far rail, 
prior to the arrival of a train. Required clearing sight distance along both directions of the track, 
from the stopped position of the vehicle, is dependent upon the maximum train speed and the 
acceleration characteristics of the “design” vehicle (WB-65 semi-truck).
37.
The necessary clearing sight distance at the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing 
from the northern and southern approaches is 333 feet. The available clearing sight distance 
from NP Railroad is 140 feet in the northwest quadrant and over 2,000 in the remaining 
quadrants. The clearing sight distance is inadequate in the northwest quadrant.
38.
The necessary clearing sight distance at the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing 
from the eastern and western approaches on Railroad Street is 409 feet. The available clearing 
sight distance is 223 feet in the northwest quadrant, 140 feet in the northeast quadrant, 2000+ 

Docket 9020-RX-186
9
feet in the southwest quadrant, and 2000+ feet in the southeast quadrant. The clearing sight 
distance is inadequate in the northwest and northeast quadrants.
39.
At the time of the inspection, brush clearing and tree trimming was needed in the 
northwest quadrant within the railroad right-of-way.
40.
One train-vehicle accident has occurred at this crossing since 1973 with no 
injuries or fatalities.
41.
W10-1 advance warning signs were not present on NP Railroad or Railroad Street 
at the time of the inspection.
42.
Parallel tracks advance warning signs were present on Winter Street at the time of 
the inspection.
43.
There are currently no visible stop lines at the crossing; stop lines are required on 
Railroad Street (eastern and western approaches are paved) but are not required on Winter Street 
(northern and southern approaches are unpaved). The use of stop lines should adhere to the 
standards and guidance in the WMUTCD4. Since the track has a 16-degree RHF skew at the 
Railroad Street approaches, stop lines should be installed on both Railroad Street approaches at 
54 feet from the near rail as measured along the Railroad Street centerline, so drivers don’t stop 
in the foul.
44.
The Number of Tracks (R15-2P) plaque on the southern crossbuck assembly was 
cracked and non-reflective at the time of the inspection.
4 WMUTCD 2023 8C.03.01, 8C.03.02 and 8C.03.03 (crossings with passive warning devices). 

Docket 9020-RX-186
10
45.
The crossing is presently protected with reflective crossbucks and yield signs only 
on NP Railroad. Conditions warrant maintaining the passive warning devices at this crossing 
because of the low train and vehicle speeds and exposure factor. 
46.
To promote public safety, it is necessary to replace the Yield sign with a Stop sign 
on the northern approach, maintain a Yield sign on the southern approach, and install 
supplemental crossbuck assemblies with Stop signs on eastbound and westbound Railroad Street. 
Conclusions of Law
The Office of the Commissioner of Railroads has jurisdiction over this matter under Wis. 
Stat. §§ 195.03(2), 195.28, and 195.29 and enters this order consistent with the findings of fact.
Order
Ajax Road
1.
The BNSF shall open a new crossing number in the U.S. DOT inventory for the 
northern industrial track at Ajax Road and update the existing Ajax Road crossing (Crossing 
No. 082642N / MP 4.206) in the U.S. DOT inventory to include only the southern yard track by 
August 10, 2026.
2.
The BNSF shall install and maintain reflective crossbucks (R15-1) and Yield (R1-
2) signs on each approach to the southern yard track crossing of Ajax Road (082642N) by 
August 10, 2026. 
3.
The BNSF shall install and maintain reflective crossbucks (R15-1), Yield (R1-2) 
signs, and Emergency Notification System (ENS) (I13-1) signs reflecting the new crossing 
number on each approach to the crossing of the northern industrial track with Ajax Road by 
August 10, 2026. 

Docket 9020-RX-186
11
4.
The BNSF shall provide the Office with a copy of the updated U.S. DOT 
inventory form for the southern yard track crossing of Ajax Road (082642N) and the U.S. DOT 
inventory form for the new crossing number of the northern industrial track crossing of Ajax 
Road by August 10, 2026.
5.
The BNSF shall remove the Number of Tracks (R15-2P) plaques from the 
crossbuck assemblies at the crossing of the southern yard track (082642N) and northern 
industrial track with Ajax Road by August 10, 2026. 
6.
The BNSF shall clear brush and trees from its right-of-way for 330 feet down the 
tracks in each direction from the crossing of the northern industrial track with Ajax Road by 
September 8, 2026. 
7.
The City of Superior shall clear brush and trim trees within its highway 
right-of-way for 330 feet down the highway in each direction from the crossing of the northern 
industrial track with Ajax Road by September 8, 2026. 
8.
The City of Superior shall install and maintain AWS in the southbound traffic 
lane for the crossing of the northern industrial track with Ajax Road and in the northbound 
traffic lane for the crossing of the southern yard track with Ajax Road at a distance in 
accordance with MUTCD standards by August 10, 2026.
9.
The City of Superior shall install and maintain "parallel tracks" advance warning 
signs [Sign W10-4 in the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)] on Railroad 
Street for eastbound traffic at a distance from the intersection in accordance with MUTCD 
standards by August 10, 2026. 

Docket 9020-RX-186
12
10.
The City of Superior shall install and maintain additional signs to inform 
motorists of the distance to cross the tracks in accordance with the MUTCD by November 9, 
2026. 
Winter Street at NP Railroad (Crossing No. 082644C)
11.
The BNSF shall relocate and maintain the crossbuck assemblies on the northern 
and southern approaches to the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing 15 feet from the near rail 
and in accordance with the WMUTCD by August 10, 2026. 
12.
The BNSF shall install and maintain a Number of Tracks (R15-2P) plaque on the 
southern crossbuck assembly at the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing by August 10, 
2026.
13.
The City of Superior shall install and maintain Stop lines on both Railroad Street 
approaches to the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing by August 10, 2026.
14.
The BNSF shall install and maintain new supplemental reflective crossbucks 
(R15-1) aligned with the stop lines, Number of Tracks (R15-2P) plaques, and ENS I13-1 signs 
on both Railroad Street approaches to the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing by August 10, 
2026.
15.
The City of Superior, in coordination with BNSF, shall install and maintain Stop 
signs on the northern crossbuck assembly on NP Railroad and on the new eastern and western 
crossbuck assemblies on Railroad Street by August 10, 2026.
16.
The BNSF shall clear brush and trees from its right-of-way for 330 feet down the 
tracks in each direction from the Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing by September 8, 
2026.

Docket 9020-RX-186
13
17.
The City of Superior shall install and maintain AWS (W10-1) for southbound 
traffic of NP Railroad and in the eastbound and westbound traffic lanes of Railroad Street for the 
Winter Street at NP Railroad crossing at a distance in accordance with MUTCD standards by 
August 10, 2026.
18.
The City of Superior shall install and maintain parallel track W10-2 signs in the 
eastbound and westbound traffic lanes of Railroad Street at a distance in accordance with 
MUTCD standards by August 10, 2026.
19.
The City of Superior shall maintain "parallel tracks" advance warning signs on 
Winter Street for eastbound and westbound traffic at a distance from the Winter Street at 
NP Railroad intersection in accordance with MUTCD standards.
20.
The BNSF shall file an updated FRA inventory form 6180.71 listing the NP 
Railroad crossing as a public crossing and provide the Office with a copy by August 10, 2026.
21.
The City of Superior shall file a petition with the Office to establish a public 
crossing of the NP Railroad crossing by September 8, 2026. 
22.
Notwithstanding any other cost apportionment in this order, the BNSF shall pay 
the expenses attributable to this investigation under Wis. Stat. § 195.60.
23.
If any interested party objects to this order and requests a hearing within 20 days 
of the date of this order in writing, the Office will determine the nature of the objection and may 
hold a public hearing.
24.
This Final Decision is effective one day after service.
25.
Jurisdiction is retained.

PETITION FOR REHEARING
If this decision is an order following a contested case proceeding as defined in Wis. Stat. 
§ 227.01(3), a person aggrieved by the decision has a right to petition the Office of the 
Commissioner of Railroads (Office) for rehearing within 20 days of the date of service of this 
decision. Wis. Stat. § 227.49. The date of service is shown on the first page. The petition for 
rehearing must be filed with the Office and served on the parties. The filing of a petition for 
rehearing does not suspend or delay the order’s effective date. Wis. Stat. § 227.49(2). An appeal 
of this decision may also be taken directly to circuit court through the filing of a petition for 
judicial review. It is not necessary to first petition for rehearing.
PETITION FOR JUDICIAL REVIEW
A person aggrieved by this decision has a right to petition for judicial review as provided in Wis. 
Stat. § 227.53. The petition must be filed in circuit court and served upon the Commissioner by 
personal service or certified mail within 30 days of the date of service of this decision if there has 
been no petition for rehearing. If a timely petition for rehearing has been filed, the petition for 
judicial review must be filed within 30 days of the date of service of the order finally disposing 
of the petition for rehearing, or within 30 days after the final disposition of the petition for 
rehearing by operation of law pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 227.49(5), whichever is sooner. If an 
untimely petition for rehearing is filed, the 30-day period to petition for judicial review 
commences the date the Office serves its original decision.5 The Office must be named as 
respondent in the petition for judicial review.
If this decision is an order denying rehearing, a person aggrieved who wishes to appeal must 
seek judicial review rather than rehearing. A second petition for rehearing is not permitted.

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WISCONSIN
Simplified Rate Case for the City of Black River Falls, as a Water 
Public Utility, Jackson County, Wisconsin
550-WQ-106
FINAL DECISION
Introduction
On June 3, 2026, Black River Falls Municipal Electric and Water (applicant) filed an 
application for a water rate increase under Wis. Stat. § 196.193, a simplified rate case (SRC) process 
that does not require a hearing. (PSC REF#: 593229.) The Commission reviewed the information 
submitted by the applicant in support of its application and determined that the water rate increase, 
as requested, is justified.
Findings of Fact
1.
The revenue increase is calculated by multiplying the applicant’s prior year revenue 
from sales of utility service by the rate increase factor (3.0 percent) set by the Commission on 
February 19, 2026 and effective March 1, 2026. (PSC REF#: 580421.)
2.
The revenue increase, combined with the applicant’s prior year net operating 
income, results in an overall rate of return that does not exceed 6.4 percent, the overall rate of return 
for municipally owned water or combined water and sewer public utilities set by the Commission 
on February 19, 2026 and effective March 1, 2026. (PSC REF#: 580421.)
3.
The effective date of the rate increase is not less than 12 months from the effective 
date of a previous SRC increase and is not less than 45 days from the date of this application.
4.
The applicant’s last rate increase authorized pursuant to a hearing under Wis. Stat. 
§ 196.20 has been in effect for at least one calendar year (i.e., January through December).

5.
The applicant has fewer than 4,000 customers, and the total of all prior rate increases 
granted since the last hearing under Wis. Stat. § 196.20 does not result in rates that are more than 40 
percent higher than the base rates previously authorized by a hearing under Wis. Stat. § 196.20.
6.
The applicant notified all its customers of the proposed rate increase.
(PSC REF#: 593229.)
Conclusions of Law
1.
The Commission has jurisdiction under Wis. Stat. §§ 196.02, 196.193, and 196.39, 
and Wis. Admin. Code ch. PSC 185.
2.
The Commission has authority under Wis. Stat. § 15.02(4) to delegate to the 
Administrator of the Division of Water Utility Regulation and Analysis (Division Administrator) 
those functions vested by law as enumerated above and has delegated the authority to issue this 
Final Decision to the Division Administrator.
Order
1.
The applicant shall increase its rates for general service and public fire protection 
uniformly by the 3.0 percent rate increase factor.
2.
The new rates will be effective August 1, 2026 and will be on file with the 
Commission as Amendment 37, provided that the applicant makes a copy of the new rates available 
to the public before this date by placing a copy of the new rates at locations where customer 
payments are accepted, on the applicant’s website, or in a form and place that is otherwise readily 
accessible to the public. If a copy of the new rates is not made available to the public by this date, 
the new rates shall take effect on the date they are so made available.
3.
The applicant shall inform each customer of the new rates authorized by this order.
4.
The applicant’s current rates and rules shall be available for public inspection.

5.
The applicant shall keep on permanent file all its previous rates.
6.
Jurisdiction is retained.
7.
This order is effective one day after the date of service.

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WISCONSIN
Application of Town of Troy, Troy Center Sanitary District No 1, 
Walworth County, Wisconsin, as a Water Public Utility, for 
Authority to Change its Method of Cost Recovery for Providing 
Public Fire Protection Service
5960-PFP-100
FINAL DECISION
This is the Final Decision in the Class 1 proceeding conducted by the Public Service 
Commission (Commission) on the application of the Troy Center Sanitary District #1 (applicant) 
for approval to revise its method of cost recovery for providing public fire protection (PFP) 
service. This application is APPROVED, subject to conditions.
Introduction
The applicant applied to the Commission on December 22, 2025, for authority to revise 
its method of cost recovery for providing PFP service. (PSC REF#: 571381.) Pursuant to due 
notice, the Commission held an audiovisual hearing on June 16, 2026, before Administrative 
Law Judge Michael E. Newmark. The parties, for purposes of review under Wis. Stat. §§ 227.47 
and 227.53, are listed in Appendix A. The applicant is the only party to this proceeding.
Findings of Fact
1.
The applicant’s presently authorized rates provide for a total PFP charge of 
$15,397. This charge is comprised of an annual municipal PFP charge of $15,397 collected 
through property taxes. The applicant does not currently collect any PFP revenue through a 
direct charge on water customers’ bills.
2.
The rates set forth in Appendix B will permit the applicant to recover $15,397 of 
its PFP costs through direct charges on the water bills to all the applicant’s general service and 
PSC REF#:597171
Public Service Commission of Wisconsin 
RECEIVED: 7/10/2026 8:35:01 AM

Docket 5960-PFP-100
2
non-general service customers. The applicant will no longer recover PFP costs through an 
annual municipal PFP charge.
Conclusions of Law
1.
The applicant is a municipal public utility as defined in Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5)(a).
2.
The Commission has authority under Wis. Stat. §§ 196.02(1); 196.03(1) and (3); 
196.19; 196.20; 196.22; 196.37(1), (2), and (3); 196.395; and 196.40 to authorize the applicant to 
revise its method of recovering PFP costs.
3.
The Commission has authority under Wis. Stat. § 15.02(4) to delegate to the 
Administrator of the Division of Water Utility Regulation and Analysis (Division Administrator) 
those functions vested by law as enumerated above and has delegated the authority to issue this 
Order to the Division Administrator.
Opinion
At present, the applicant recovers a total PFP charge of $15,397. This charge is comprised 
of an annual municipal PFP charge of $15,397 collected through property taxes by the Town of 
Troy (Town). The applicant requested to change its tariff to allow the entire PFP cost of $15,397 to 
be collected through direct PFP charges on general service customers’ water bills. This request is in 
conformance with Wis. Stat. § 196.03(3)(b), which provides municipalities the option to recover all 
or a portion of the PFP costs from water general service customers. On December 22, 2025, the 
applicant submitted its Resolution authorizing this change to the Commission. (PSC REF#: 
571381).

Commission staff submitted a proposal that provides for recovering all of the applicant’s 
PFP costs by direct billing its water general service customers based on the equivalent meters 
method. The summary of these rates appears in the record as Ex.-PSC-PFP Tariff Changes. (PSC 
REF#: 588996.) As a result of the request to change the method of collecting PFP charges, an 
average Residential customer’s bill with a ⅝-inch or ¾-inch meter who uses 10,000 gallons of water 
per quarter will increase from $99.40 to $166.93, or 67.94 percent. Prior to the hearing, 
Commission staff provided the applicant with Commission staff’s proposed rates for review, and the 
applicant had no objection to these rates.
As requested, authorized rates set forth in Appendix B, Schedule F-1, provide for PFP rates 
that reflect the applicant’s request and are consistent with the Commission’s standard methodology 
for calculating PFP charges based on equivalent meters. These rates are reasonable and just. All 
customers will be required to pay an appropriate amount for the service provided.
Schedule Mg-2, General Service Suburban, which is intended to recover costs related to 
providing PFP to water customers residing outside the corporate limits of the municipality, is not 
applicable when a utility bills PFP charges to these customers directly. Accordingly, Schedule Mg-
2 is removed from the applicant’s filed water tariff.
Unresolved Billing Issues Related to Direct PFP Charges
Under its current tariff, Schedule F-1, Public Fire Protection Service, the applicant collects 
PFP revenue through an annual municipal PFP charge of $15,397 collected through property taxes 
by the Town. During the course of this proceeding, Commission staff discovered that the applicant 
was not billing the Town pursuant to Schedule F-1 of its current tariff. This was discussed at the 
public and party hearing session on June 16, 2026, with Commission staff offering additional 
comments through testimony at the hearing session. As developed through testimony, the applicant 

Docket 5960-PFP-100
4
was prematurely collecting PFP revenue through direct PFP charges on general service customers’ 
water bills without Commission approval.
Wisconsin Stat. § 196.22 requires utilities to bill according to the rates in their tariff and 
Wis. Stat. § 196.635 limits utilities ability to back bill to only include those charges incurred within 
the past 24 months. In these situations, utilities typically review past billing errors and issue back-
bills to all customers that it billed incorrectly within 24 months from the issuance date of the back-
bill.
For any customer the applicant overcharged, the Commission may order that the applicant 
issue a refund for the full period of inaccuracy. The applicant would need to identify and show the 
adjustments separately per Wis. Admin. Code § PSC 185.33(14)(a) and provide any refund in 
accordance with Wis. Admin. Code § PSC 185.35(5).
Within 45 days of the date of this Final Decision, the applicant must back-bill the PFP 
charges per the terms of the applicant’s tariff for a two-year period from the date of billing and 
refund for the full period of inaccuracy that the applicant overcharged the customers. In addition, 
the applicant must file in this proceeding a summary of the back-bills and refunds related to 
direct PFP charges within 45 days of the date of this Final Decision.
Public Comments
One customer filed a comment on the Commission’s Electronic Records Filing (ERF) 
system concerning transfer of the PFP charges from a municipal charge to direct charges on 
customer bills. The customer expressed concern regarding the applicant’s ability to provide 
adequate PFP service. In addition, the customer questioned the applicant’s current recovery of 
the PFP charge and the unresolved billing issues identified in this decision. The Commission 
appreciates the customer’s concerns. The Commission concludes that the rates as proposed by 

Docket 5960-PFP-100
5
Commission staff would provide a reasonable and nondiscriminatory recovery of the PFP charge 
and are in conformance with Wis. Stat. § 196.03(3)(b). Accordingly, the Commission approves 
Commission staff’s proposed tariff changes as shown in Ex.-PSC-PFP Tariff Changes of the 
hearing record.
Effective Date
The applicant bills on a quarterly basis. Pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 196.19, the changes in rates 
and associated tariff provisions that are authorized in this Final Decision take effect no sooner than 
one day after the date of service, provided these rates and tariff provisions are filed with the 
Commission and the applicant makes a copy of the new rates available to the public before this date 
by placing a copy of the new rates at locations where customer payments are accepted, on the 
applicant’s website, or in a form and place that is otherwise readily accessible to the public.
Order
1.
This Final Decision takes effect one day after the date of service.
2.
The authorized rate changes and tariff provisions shall take effect no sooner than 
one day after the day the applicant has: (a) filed these rates and tariff provisions with the 
Commission; and (b) made them available to the public at locations where customer payments 
are accepted, on the applicant’s website, or in a form and place that is otherwise readily 
accessible to the public, pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 196.19 and Wis. Admin. Code § PSC 
185.33(1)(f). If a copy of the new rates and tariff provisions is not made available to the public 
when they are filed with the Commission, the new rates and tariff provisions shall take effect one 
day after the day they are made available to the public.
3.
The rates approved in this docket shall take effect no later than 90 days from the 
service date of this Final Decision or as directed by the Commission or Commission staff.

Docket 5960-PFP-100
6
4.
Within 45 days of the date of this Final Decision, the applicant shall correct any 
billing issues related to the direct PFP charges and submit a summary of the back-bills and 
refunds related to direct PFP charges.
5.
Jurisdiction is retained.

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WISCONSIN
Joint Application of Wisconsin Gas LLC and Wisconsin Electric Power 
Company for Approval of an Affiliated Interest Agreement
5-AU-122
FINAL DECISION
This is the Final Decision on the application of Wisconsin Gas LLC (WG) and Wisconsin 
Electric Power Company (WEPCO) (together, applicants) for approval of an affiliated interest 
transaction (transaction) between the applicants to enable the transfer of active employee benefits 
within the WEC Energy Group, Inc. Retiree Welfare Trust (trust) from the WG sub-account to the 
WEPCO sub-account. The application is APPROVED, as conditioned by this Final Decision.
Introduction
On August 26, 2025, the applicants filed an application requesting approval of an 
affiliated interest transaction between the applicants to enable the transfer of active employee 
benefits within the WEC Energy Group, Inc. trust. (PSC REF#: 559542.)
On January 9, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Investigation in this docket. 
(PSC REF#: 572587.) The Notice instructed those persons desiring to become a party to file for 
intervention no later than 14 days from the date of service. No party requested to intervene in 
this docket. The Commission’s notice stated that the Commission intended to conduct its 
investigation without a hearing. No hearing was requested, required, or held. On March 6, 2026, 
the Chairperson of the Commission granted a 90-day extension under Wis. Stat. § 196.52(3)(d)2. 
for the Commission to take final action in this docket. The new deadline for taking final action 
is July 8, 2026. (PSC REF#: 582183.)

1.

2.

conditioned upon the reserved power of the Commission to terminate or to revise and amend the

3
terms and conditions thereof, if, when, and as needed to protect and promote the public interest 
as provided in Wis. Stat. § 196.52(5).
Conclusions of Law
1.
The Commission has authority to review and approve the transaction under Wis. 
Stat. § 196.52(3) and the authority to condition its approval of such transaction under Wis. Stat. 
§§ 196.395 and 196.52(5).
2.
The transaction (PSC REF#: 559542) is reasonable and consistent with the public 
interest, subject to the terms and conditions in this Final Decision, which are necessary to protect 
the public interest.
Legal Standard
The applicants request Commission approval of the proposed transactions under 
Wis. Stat. § 196.52 because the applicants are affiliated interests. Under Wis. Stat. § 196.52, any 
person owning or holding directly or indirectly 5 percent or more of the voting securities of a public 
utility is an “affiliated interest” of that public utility. The Commission’s approval is guided by 
Wisconsin Stat. § 196.52(3)(a), which states:
[t]he commission shall approve a contract or arrangement [between affiliated 
interests] . . . only if it shall clearly appear and be established upon investigation 
that it is reasonable and consistent with the public interest. The commission may 
not approve any contract or arrangement unless satisfactory proof is submitted to 
the commission of the cost to the affiliated interest of rendering the services or of 
furnishing the property or service to each public utility or of the cost to the public 
utility of rendering the services or of furnishing the property or service to each 
affiliated interest.

Docket 5-AU-122

4
Discussion
The applicants sought an affiliated interest transaction to enable the transfer of active 
employee benefits from the Voluntary Employees’ Beneficiary Association (VEBA) from 
WG sub-accounts to the WEPCO sub-account. The transaction would make a dollar-for-dollar 
exchange of WG’s interests in the sub-account for union medical and life benefits within the 
trust for cash from WEPCO. The trust was established in January 2021 as a result of a merger of 
two former VEBA’s, the WEC Life VEBA (life VEBA) and the WEC Union Medical VEBA 
(medical VEBA). Merging these separate VEBA’s into one trust allowed the applicants to 
utilize surplus funds from the former medical VEBA to eliminate underfunding in the former life 
VEBA. Thus, utilizing the surplus funds in this manner provided the applicants with the means 
to avoid the potential for the excess funds to be subject to excise tax. 
WG’s interest in its sub-account is currently overfunded by approximately $80 million. 
If the VEBA funds are not utilized to pay qualified benefits, those funds will revert back to WG 
and a 100 percent excise tax would be triggered as well as potential Unrelated Business Income 
Tax on any investment income generated by the excess funds. The overfunding of the WG fund 
is due to several factors including stronger than expected asset returns, changes in retiree health 
plan design and coverage, and better than expected health outcomes for WG’s retiree population 
as stated in response to Commission staff data request PSCW-TMC-1.1. (PSC REF#: 563871.) 
WEPCO’s interest in the plan is overfunded by approximately $10 million. Without the 
proposed transaction, WEPCO would need to fund active union employee medical benefits in 
excess of the existing $10 million in surplus funds using corporate cash instead of the additional 
surplus funds within the trust. To meet the needs of the applicants and to minimize the tax 

Docket 5-AU-122

5
impact to WG’s customers, the applicants propose exchanging $75 million of WG’s interest in 
the VEBA trust assets for $75 million in cash from WEPCO. WEPCO will use the surplus funds 
in the trust to pay active union employee’s medical and life benefits while WG will reduce its 
surplus thereby avoiding excise and Unrelated Business Income Tax on the overfunded balance. 
As such, the Commission finds the proposed transaction is reasonable and consistent with the 
public interest pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 196.52(3). The Commission therefore approves the 
transaction, subject to the conditions discussed below. 
In its approval of prior affiliated interest agreements, the Commission has found it 
reasonable and in the public interest to include several general conditions and the Commission 
finds it reasonable to include those here:
1.
The applicants shall obtain Commission approval prior to the effective date of any 
suspensions, modifications, or termination of the transaction.
2.
The Commission shall have full access to all books and records related to the 
underlying services under the transaction.
3.
Approval of the transaction is not a determination by the Commission that the 
charges are just and reasonable.
4.
The applicants shall submit to the Commission within 30 days of execution all 
final accounting journal entries, by FERC Account.
Every order of the Commission approving a contract or arrangement under Wis. Stat. 
§ 196.52(5) is also statutorily required to include a condition like the following: 
5.
Approval of the transaction granted herein is expressly conditioned upon the 
reserved power of the Commission to terminate or to revise and amend the terms

6
and conditions thereof, if, when, and as needed to protect and promote the public 
interest as provided in Wis. Stat. § 196.52(5).
The Commission also finds it reasonable to include these conditions in its approval of the 
transaction in this docket.
Order
1.
The transaction as filed on August 26, 2025, (PSC REF#: 559542), as described in 
the Final Decision, is approved as conditioned by this Final Decision.
2.
The applicants shall obtain Commission approval prior to the effective date of any 
suspensions, modifications, or termination of the transaction.
3.
The Commission shall have full access to all books and records related to the 
underlying services under the transaction.
4.
Approval of the transaction is not a determination by the Commission that the 
charges are just and reasonable.
5.
The applicants shall submit to the Commission within 30 days of execution all 
final accounting journal entries, by FERC Account.
6.
Approval of the transaction granted herein is expressly conditioned upon the 
reserved power of the Commission to terminate or to revise and amend the terms and conditions 
thereof, if, when, and as needed to protect and promote the public interest as provided in Wis. 
Stat. § 196.52(5).
7.
This Final Decision is effective one day after the date of service.
8.
Jurisdiction is retained.

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WISCONSIN
Joint Application of Wisconsin Public Service Corporation and 
Wisconsin Electric Power Company for Blanket Approval of Affiliated 
Interest Agreements Related to Capacity-Only Transactions
5-AE-261
FINAL DECISION
This is the Final Decision on the joint application of Wisconsin Public Service 
Corporation (WPSC) and Wisconsin Electric Power Company (WEPCO) (together, applicants), 
for blanket approval of an affiliated interest template agreement to buy and sell capacity between 
the applicants, and to treat the sale of capacity as an opportunity sale. The application is 
APPROVED with conditions. 
Introduction
On November 15, 2024, the applicants applied for approval of an affiliated interest 
template agreement (Agreement) for blanket approval to buy and sell capacity as needed 
between the applicants pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 196.52. (PSC REF#: 524128 confidential, 
PSC REF#: 524129 public.) The applicants also requested to treat the capacity transactions as 
opportunity sales consistent with Wis. Admin. Code ch. PSC 117.
The Commission issued a Notice of Investigation on January 9, 2026. (PSC REF#: 
572591.) The Commission’s notice stated that the Commission intended to conduct its 
investigation without a hearing. No party requested to intervene in this docket. No hearing was 
requested, required, or held. Pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 196.52(3)(d)2., the Commission is required 
to take final action on the application within 90 days after the Commission issues a notice 
opening the docket, unless an extension of time is granted by the Commission Chairperson. The 
PSC REF#:596888
Public Service Commission of Wisconsin 
RECEIVED: 7/7/2026 2:35:00 PM

Docket 5-AE-261

2
initial 90-day deadline for Commission action would have expired on April 9, 2026. On 
March 5, 2026, the Chairperson of the Commission found good cause to grant a 90-day 
extension under Wis. Stat. § 196.52(3)(d)2 for the Commission to take final action in this docket. 
(PSC REF#: 582505.) The new deadline for taking final action is July 8, 2026.
On June 18, 2026, Commission staff issued a memorandum analyzing the request and 
solicited comments from the applicants and the public. (PSC REF#: 594623.) Comments on the 
Commission staff memorandum were submitted by the applicants. (PSC REF#: 595247.) The 
Commission considered the applicants’ request at its open meeting on July 2, 2026.
Findings of Fact
1.
WPSC is a public utility as defined in Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5), engaged in the 
business of providing electric and natural gas services.
2.
WEPCO is a public utility as defined in Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5), engaged in the 
business of providing electric, natural gas, and steam services. 
3.
The applicants’ parent company, WEC Energy Group, Inc., owns or controls 
more than 5 percent of the voting securities of the applicants.
4.
The applicants are affiliated interests pursuant to Wis. Stat. §§ 196.52 and 
196.795.
5.
It is reasonable that the applicants obtain Commission approval prior to the 
effective date of any suspension, modification, or termination of the Agreement 
6.
It is reasonable that the Commission shall have full access to all books and 
records relating to the underlying services under the transaction. 

Docket 5-AE-261

3
7.
It is reasonable that approval of the Agreement is not a determination by the 
Commission that the charges are just and reasonable for any Wisconsin jurisdiction ratemaking 
purposes.
8.
It is reasonable that approval of the arrangements granted herein is expressly 
conditioned upon the reserved power of the Commission to terminate or to revise and amend its 
terms and conditions thereof, if, when, and as needed to protect and promote the public interest as 
provided in Wis. Stat. §196.52(5). 
9.
It is reasonable that the applicants may not use any capacity transactions under the 
Agreement to directly meet the needs of very large customers (VLC).
10.
It is reasonable that the capacity price set under the proposed Agreement shall 
require the Auction Clearing Prices (ACP) that are used to establish the capacity price of the 
Agreement to be the results from Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) 
Planning Resource Auctions (PRA) that had the same auction methodology as the one expected 
over the term of the Agreement.
Conclusions of Law
1.
The Commission has authority to review and approve the affiliated interest 
agreements under Wis. Stat. § 196.52(3) and the authority to condition its approval of such 
agreements under Wis. Stat. §§ 196.395 and 196.52(5).
2.
The Agreement (PSC REF#: 524130 confidential, PSC REF#: 524131 public) is 
reasonable and consistent with the public interest, subject to the terms and conditions stated in 
this Final Decision, which are necessary to protect the public interest.

Docket 5-AE-261

4
Background
The applicants sought blanket approval of an affiliated interest agreement under Wis. Stat. 
§ 196.52 to buy and sell capacity as needed between the applicants. The applicants filed the 
Agreement for a capacity transaction, as Attachment A to the application, where WEPCO would 
act as the buyer and WPSC would act as the seller. (PSC REF#: 524130 confidential, PSC REF#: 
524131 public.) Under the Agreement either applicant would sell available capacity to the other 
applicant in the form of Zonal Resource Credits, in accordance with MISO tariffs and the MISO 
Resource Adequacy Business Practices Manual. The term of a given transaction would be based 
on the receiving applicants’ actual capacity needs for a given planning year on a short-term basis, 
up to three years unless terminated by one of the applicants. The applicants stated that the 
proposed transactions would provide capacity at a price that would be considered competitive 
with the current capacity market in the MISO North footprint and would reflect a similar 
arms-length transaction between two unaffiliated parties. Sales of capacity under the Agreement 
would be considered a capacity opportunity sale, with the revenue from the sale offsetting the 
seller’s monitored fuel costs.
The applicants stated that overall, the MISO PRA has resulted in volatile prices. The 
applicants stated that MISO’s change to the seasonal construct is a source of uncertainty and that 
customers face the risk of high capacity prices due to increasing retirements of older fossil-fueled 
generation and delays in bringing newer generation sources online. The applicants proposed the 
following seasonal capacity pricing formulas, one for the summer season and one for the 
remaining seasons. Both formulas are based on an averaging of two historical planning years 

Docket 5-AE-261

5
and the MISO Cost of New Entry (CONE). (PSC REF#: 524128 confidential, PSC REF#: 
524129 public at 9.) 
Under the Agreement, pricing for the Prompt Planning Year (PY) would remain in effect 
for the entire term (up to three years) of the Agreement. Once the Agreement terminates or 
expires, the same formula would be used to re-calculate the price for a future year under a 
renewed Agreement.
The applicants stated the Agreement would provide benefits to both applicants and the 
Agreement would assist the applicants to manage uncertainty related to Seasonal Accredited 
Capacity (SAC) and minimize exposure to MISO PRA price uncertainty for both the buying and 
selling utility.
The applicants also sought approval to treat the capacity transactions as opportunity sales 
consistent with Wis. Admin. Code ch. PSC 117. 
Legal Standard
The applicants request Commission approval of the proposed Agreement under Wis. Stat. 
§ 196.52 because the applicants are affiliated interests as defined therein. Under Wis. Stat. § 
196.52, any person owning or holding directly or indirectly 5 percent or more of the voting 
securities of a public utility is an “affiliated interest” of that public utility. The Commission’s 
approval is guided by Wisconsin Stat. § 196.52(3)(a), which states:
[t]he commission shall approve a contract or arrangement [between affiliated 
interests] . . . only if it shall clearly appear and be established upon investigation 
that it is reasonable and consistent with the public interest. The commission may 
not approve any contract or arrangement unless satisfactory proof is submitted to 
the commission of the cost to the affiliated interest of rendering the services or of 
furnishing the property or service to each public utility or of the cost to the public 
utility of rendering the services or of furnishing the property or service to each 
affiliated interest.

Docket 5-AE-261

6
Discussion
Under the proposed Agreement, the purchase and sale of capacity between the applicants 
would work in both directions, with either applicant being both a potential buyer and potential 
seller. In response to Commission staff data request PSCW-DMG-3.4 regarding if the 
movement of capacity would be bi-directional in practice, the applicants stated that the proposed 
Agreement in this proceeding will only be used for capacity transactions needed to fulfill 
WEPCOs non-VLC demand obligation. (PSC REF#: 555501.) This means that capacity 
provided by WPSC would not be used to serve VLC demand under WEPCO’s VLC and 
Bespoke Resources tariffs, thus protecting WPSC customers from subsidizing WEPCO 
customers in the event the capacity price under this Agreement is less than the VLC tariff rates.1 
This specific exclusion was not found in the proposed template agreement. (PSC REF#: 524130 
confidential, PSC REF#: 524131 public.) 
Without knowing the specific details on the respective applicants’ future capacity 
positions and how the Agreement would be used in practice, Commission staff had also 
identified that there could be scenarios where VLCs could directly or indirectly cause a capacity 
shortfall of non-VLCs. In response to Commission staff’s memorandum, the applicants asserted 
that the proposed Agreement was not drafted to benefit VLCs; however, there are scenarios 
when the non-VLCs would receive more revenue from selling excess capacity to VLCs than they 
would by simply accepting the ACP and therefore suggested modifications to Commission 
staff’s proposed order condition. (PSC REF#: 595247.) The Commission acknowledges the 
potential for scenarios where the capacity transactions could indirectly be used to serve VLCs 
1 Final Decision docket 6630-TE-113 (PSC REF#: 591873)

Docket 5-AE-261

7
and the potential benefits associated with such scenarios. Based on the applicants’ assertion 
regarding the intended use, as well as Commission staff concerns, the Commission finds it 
reasonable to impose the following order condition, modifying Commission staff’s original 
suggestion to remove the reference of the word “indirectly”:
1.
The applicants may not use any capacity transactions authorized under the 
Agreement to directly meet the needs of VLCs. 
Capacity Pricing
The capacity price calculations using the formulas proposed by the applicants shown in 
the application and in response to PSCW-KAC-2.8 (PSC REF#: 593449 confidential, 
PSC REF#: 593450) were for a 2025 PY and based on the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 MISO 
PRA ACP. These were the two most recent historical years available at the time of the 
application. These results were also based on MISO’s previous vertical demand curve 
methodology for calculating ACPs. However, beginning with the 2025-2026 PRA, MISO 
switched to the Reliability-Based Demand Curve (RBDC) methodology. MISO also provided 
simulated results for the 2024-2025 PRA, which restated what the 2024-2025 ACPs would have 
been had the new RBDC methodology been used.
Commission staff noted that with this change in methodology, ACPs from historical 
PRAs based on the vertical demand curve are not comparable to more recent and future PRAs 
based on the RBDC. Therefore, Commission staff identified that any analysis that uses historical 
PRA results used to forecast or set future prices should be based on RBDC-based historical 
results in order to be consistent with the forward-looking expectations. Based on the change in 
methodology and the fact that the request is for blanket approval, the Commission finds it 

Docket 5-AE-261

8
reasonable to provide protection for the future in scenarios where the MISO auction 
methodology would change. As such, the Commission finds it reasonable to impose the 
following order condition: 
2.
The capacity price set under the proposed Agreement shall require the ACPs that 
are used to establish the capacity price of the Agreement to be the results from MISO PRAs that 
had the same auction methodology as the one expected over the term of the Agreement.
Using the applicants’ proposed formulas, Commission staff calculated the seasonal 
capacity prices based on actual MISO PRA results from 2025-2026 and the RBDC simulation 
results provided from MISO for 2024-2025. Table 1 below shows the updated data and results.

FINAL DECISION
This is the Final Decision in the Class 1 proceeding conducted by the Public Service 
Commission (Commission) on the application of Clayton Municipal Water Utility (applicant) for 
approval to increase water rates. This application is APPROVED, subject to conditions.
Introduction
The applicant applied to the Commission on February 13, 2026 for authority to increase 
water rates. The Commission authorized the applicant’s last conventional rate case (CRC) 
change in docket 1150-WR-103 in a Final Decision dated January 3, 2022. Since that Final 
Decision, the Commission authorized an additional rate increase through the simplified rate case 
(SRC) process in 2025. The applicant filed for a rate increase after receiving letters from 
Commission staff outlining Commission staff’s concerns regarding the applicant’s financial 
integrity. (PSC REF#: 578796.) In addition, the applicant requested the rate increase to recover 
increasing operation and maintenance costs. In this rate case, the final overall rate change 
authorized is $27,649, or a 17.11 percent increase over current rates, for the test year ending 
December 31, 2026.
Pursuant to due notice, the Commission held an audiovisual hearing on June 30, 2026 
before Administrative Law Judge Michael E. Newmark. The parties, for purposes of review 
under Wis. Stat. § 227.53, are listed in Appendix A as required by Wis. Stat § 227.47. The 
applicant is the only party to this proceeding.

Findings of Fact
1.

operating revenues of $163,477 for the 2026 test year. These rates fall short of the test year 
revenue needed by $27,649 and are unreasonable.

Capital Structure
The Commission utilizes a rate of return on net investment rate base (ROR) to ensure 
utilities can cover interest on outstanding debt, earn a return on equity capital that fairly 
compensates for investment risk, and preserve and attract capital in their long-term operations. 
The Commission calculates a benchmark ROR weekly based on a three-month rolling average of 
municipal bond rates and determines a floor annually. The benchmark ROR at the time 
Commission staff finalized the revenue requirement exhibit for this case was 6.40 percent.
The applicant originally requested an ROR of 6.90 percent. Commission staff estimated 
the applicant’s capital employed in providing public utility service associated with the net 
investment rate base to be 100.00 percent municipal equity. The applicant did not object to using 
the benchmark ROR of 6.40 percent.
The Commission finds that a 6.40 percent ROR will provide the applicant with sufficient 
earnings to help address future capital and unforeseen operating needs and will also maintain 
confidence in the applicant’s financial integrity without resulting in customer rates that are 
excessive.
Back-bills and Refunds
Between January 10, 2022 and September 30, 2024, the applicant did not charge 178 
vacant lots within the municipality for public fire protection (PFP) as provided by its filed tariff, 
Schedule F-1, Public Fire Protection Service, and pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 196.03(3)(b). (PSC 
REF#: 586898.) If the applicant had charged the vacant lots for their PFP service, the applicant 
would have collected $17,565 more in revenue annually, which impacted its Net Operating 
Income (Loss). Wisconsin Stat. §196.635 requires that all service supplied by a public utility

for the full period of inaccuracy. On January 26, 2026, the applicant back-billed PFP service for

the applicant refunded PFP service for the 178 vacant lots for the period of January 1, 2024-

Commission staff analyzed the cost of supplying water for general service and for PFP 
service using the base-extra capacity cost allocation method. This method first allocates the 
operating expenses to the service cost functional components of base, customer, extra-capacity 
maximum-day and extra capacity maximum-hour demand, and fire protection and then to each of 
the customer classes served. Commission staff provided summaries of these analyses in 
Schedules 8 and 11 of Ex.-PSC-COSS and Rate Design, which is Commission staff’s proposal in 
the record in this proceeding. (PSC REF#: 592217.) Appendix B shows customer class revenue 
requirements resulting from the cost analysis compared with revenues at authorized rates.
Rates
Water service rates authorized in this decision will result in an estimated net operating 
income of approximately $10,262, which provides a 6.40 percent return on the water utility net 
investment rate base of $160,351. Commission staff provided the applicant with Commission 
staff’s proposed rates for review prior to the hearing, and the applicant had no objection to these 
rates.

As shown in attached Appendix B, the base-extra capacity cost allocation method results 
in a relatively wide range of increases in the charges to the various general service customer 
classes to reflect the cost of providing service to such classes. The percentage rate increase to 
any individual customer will not necessarily equal the overall percentage increase to the 
associated customer class but will depend on the specific water use of that customer.
The authorized rates as set forth in Appendix C are based on the cost of providing service 
to various customer classes or types of service. The Commission finds that the rates will result 
in all customers paying an appropriate amount for the service provided.
Commission staff computed some typical water bills for Single-Family Residential, 
Multifamily Residential, Commercial, Industrial, and Public Authority customers using 
Schedule Mg-1 to compare present rates with the new rates. That comparison is set forth in

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WISCONSIN
Application of Wisconsin Power and Light Company for Approval of an 
Agreement Renewal for Individually Contracted Natural Gas Transportation 
Service with Dairyland Power Cooperative
6680-TG-126
FINAL DECISION
This is the Final Decision in the investigation by the Public Service Commission of 
Wisconsin (Commission) for approval of an agreement renewal for individually-contracted 
natural gas transportation service provided by Wisconsin Power and Light Company (applicant) 
to its customer Dairyland Power Cooperative (DPC). The applicant’s request is GRANTED.
Introduction
On November 4, 2024, the applicant filed an application for approval of an agreement 
renewal with DPC. (PSC REF#: 523259 confidential, PSC REF#: 523260 public.) On 
December 5, 2024, the Commission issued a Notice of Investigation. (PSC REF#: 525764.)
The proposed contract in this docket is a renewal of an existing agreement for 
individually contracted natural gas transportation service between the applicant and DPC, which 
was executed on October 15, 2024. The proposed contract would be effective for 25 years. 
The previous contract for natural gas transportation services between the applicant and 
Rockgen Energy LLC, the prior owner of the facility being serviced under the contract, was also 
25 years. That contract started on October 18, 1999, and expired on October 18, 2024. The 
applicant and DPC began negotiations to replace the contract in April 2022.
The applicant is currently billing the customer under its tariff Schedule CS-1, using the 
rates in the individual customer contract, executed on October 15, 2024. (PSC REF#: 534985

PSCW-ALF-1.5.) The rate factors are billed on a monthly basis and are not prorated, similar to 
other monthly bill factors. The applicant billed DPC for October 2024 natural gas transportation 
service using the rate in effect, based on the October 1999 contract. For natural gas 
transportation service to DPC since November 2024, the customer has been billed using the 
monthly Contract Rate in the agreement executed on October 15, 2024. Pursuant to Wis. Stat. 
§ 196.194 and the applicant’s Schedule CS-1, the contract was filed within 20 days after 
execution and is effective for billing, unless adjusted by the Commission within the six-month 
review period.
Under Wis. Stat. § 196.194, the Commission may approve an individual contract between 
a natural gas utility and an individual customer if the term is no longer than five years, or a 
longer period approved by the Commission. Wisconsin Stat. § 196.194 provides that a natural 
gas utility may enter into an individual contract with a customer, if substitute natural gas services 
are available to the customer or potential customer, and the absence of such a contract will cause 
the natural gas utility to be disadvantaged. Any contract under the statute must be compensatory.
Findings of Fact
1.
It is reasonable to approve the applicant’s request for a renewed contract with DPC.
2.
The contract term is 25 years.
3.
The rate in the proposed contract is compensatory.
4.
Substitute natural gas services are available to the customer, and the absence of 
this contract reflected in the applicant’s tariff will cause the natural gas utility to be 
disadvantaged.

Docket 6680-TG-126

3
Conclusions of Law
1.
The applicant is an investor-owned natural gas public utility as defined in Wis. 
Stat. § 196.01(5)(a).
2.
The Commission has the authority under Wis. Stat § 196.194 to approve an 
individual contract.
3.
The Commission has authority under Wis. Stat. § 15.02(4) to delegate to the 
Administrator of the Division of Energy Regulation and Analysis to issue a Final Decision in this 
matter.
Opinion
The Commission established the standards for a minimum compensable rate in its 
Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, and Phase I Order in docket 5-GI-108, mailed 
December 4, 1995. The Commission specified that contracted rates, at a minimum, must exceed 
all short-run variable costs of servicing the customer, plus long-run replacement costs of plant 
that can be identified as servicing the individual customer. In addition, the contracted rate must 
be compensatory in regard to making a contribution towards long-run incremental costs (LRIC) 
of operating and maintaining the entire gas system.
In its request, the applicant included an analysis of the costs incurred to serve DPC. In its 
analysis, the applicant included the LRIC, which includes the short-run marginal costs identified 
as serving the individual customer and is the lowest level of cost recovery calculated. 
(PSC REF#: 591105 confidential, PSC REF#: 591106 public.) The minimum compensable level 
includes the LRIC plus a portion of the costs of operating and maintaining the system. The 

Docket 6680-TG-126

4
minimum compensable level is the minimum amount required to be recovered through the 
contract. The applicant also calculated the amount of fully allocated operating costs.
The applicant confirmed that substitute natural gas services are available to the customer, 
explaining that the customer could provide its own operations and maintenance of the pipeline. 
(PSC REF#: 591103 confidential, PSC REF#: 591104 public.) Therefore, the loss of this 
contract would disadvantage the applicant as the incremental costs assigned to the contract 
would be recovered though rates to other natural gas customers.
The Commission finds that substitute natural gas services are available to the customer 
and, in the absence of the contract, the applicant will be disadvantaged. The Commission also 
finds that the rates are compensatory.
Contracted rates are negotiated between the customer and the utility; therefore, they do 
not follow traditional ratemaking conventions. The structure and the level of the rate paid by the 
customer is specified in the contract executed by the customer and the company and filed with 
the Commission. The Commission finds that the rates in the applicant’s proposed replacement 
contract with DPC are compensatory because the contracted rates exceed all short-run variable 
costs of servicing the customer, plus long-run replacement costs of plant that can be identified as 
servicing the individual customer and make a contribution towards LRIC of operating and 
maintaining the system.
Order
1.
The applicant’s proposed contract is approved. The applicant is expected to 
continue to charge rates under the current contract until the replacement contract takes effect
2.
This Final Decision takes effect one day after the date of service.

PETITION FOR REHEARING

rehearing within 20 days of the date of service of this decision, as provided in Wis. Stat. § 227.49.

petition for judicial review must be filed within 30 days of the date of service of the order finally
